name: Reinforcing Feedback Loop
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: The Loop That Never Says Stop
lesson.summary: A reinforcing feedback loop is a closed causal chain with an even number of negative links, so a change to any variable in it eventually amplifies itself, producing runaway growth or runaway collapse rather than stability.
lesson.body:
Once you can draw a causal loop diagram, the next question is what kind of loop you are looking at, because the two basic types behave in opposite ways. A reinforcing feedback loop, usually labeled R on a diagram, is a closed causal chain where the net effect of going all the way around the loop points in the same direction you started. There is a simple test: count the minus signs on the arrows around the loop. If that count is even, including zero, the loop is reinforcing. Every reinforcing loop is self-amplifying: a small push in one direction gets returned to its starting point as an even larger push in the same direction, which then goes around again and comes back larger still.

The clearest intuition comes from outside quantum computing entirely. A savings account earning compound interest is a one-node reinforcing loop: your balance earns interest, the interest is added to the balance, and the larger balance earns still more interest next period. Left alone, that loop produces exponential growth, not straight line growth, because the loop is feeding its own output back in as input. The same structure describes an unchecked epidemic, where more infected people produce more new infections, or a bank run, where each withdrawal makes remaining depositors more nervous, prompting more withdrawals. None of these loops care whether growth is desirable. The loop only knows how to amplify.

Return to the four node loop from the previous chapter: impressive result to media coverage to excitement to funding to more impressive results. Every arrow in that chain was marked plus, so the minus count is zero, an even number, which makes it a reinforcing loop. That single classification explains a pattern this book will keep returning to: quantum computing funding and coverage do not merely add up year over year, they tend to compound, with each cycle of announcement and investment setting a higher baseline for the next one.

It is worth sitting with the fact that reinforcing loops are directionally neutral. The same structure that produces a boom can produce a bust, because a reinforcing loop amplifies whatever perturbation it receives, including a negative one. Imagine the same four nodes starting from a disappointing result instead of an impressive one: disappointment reduces coverage, reduced coverage cools excitement, cooled excitement shrinks funding, and shrunken funding makes future disappointing results more likely, since research starved of resources tends to underperform. That is the same loop, same signs, running in reverse, and it describes a funding winter as faithfully as it describes a hype cycle.

The one thing a reinforcing loop structurally cannot do, on its own, is stop itself. If you observe a reinforcing loop that has run for years without spiraling to infinity or collapsing to zero, something outside that loop must be restraining it: a limited pool of qualified researchers, a ceiling on how much attention any topic can hold in the press, a physical constraint like decoherence that caps how fast real capability can actually grow. That restraining structure has its own name and its own behavior, and it is the subject of the next chapter.
